title: Convergent adaptation of human lactase persistence in Africa and Europe
authors: Tishkoff SA, Reed FA, Ranciaro A, Voight BF, Babbitt CC, Silverman JS, et al.
population: Tanzanians, Kenyans and Sudanese from 43 ethnic groups, phenotyped with a 50 g lactose tolerance test
funder: L.S.B. Leakey and Wenner Gren Foundation grants; US National Science Foundation grants BSC-0196183, BSC-0552486 and IGERT-9987590; US National Institutes of Health grants R01GM076637, F32HG03801 and HG002772-1; David and Lucile Packard and Burroughs Wellcome Foundation Career Awards; Duke University Institute for Genome Sciences and Policy; Wellcome Trust.
authorConflicts: The authors declare no competing financial interests.
result: In most humans lactase-phlorizin hydrolase, which hydrolyses lactose into glucose and galactose in the small intestine, declines after weaning. Lactase persistence is inherited as a dominant trait in Europeans and its frequency exceeds 90% in Swedes and Danes, is about 50% in Spanish and French populations and about 1% in Chinese. C/T-13910 lies about 14 kb upstream of LCT within MCM6. Three African variants, G/C-14010, T/G-13915 and C/G-13907, arose on different haplotypes, are associated with lactase persistence and raise LCT promoter activity in vitro by about 18-30%; selection coefficients 0.04-0.097.
